CHRISTOPHER HERRMANN
INT. LEARNING    REFLECTIONS    RESUME   


R4 - EE598: Ind. Problems / Thesis Research

Failure and neural networks


Individual problems with Dr. Fritz was definitely the most unique course that I took through my time in the UB graduate program. The original goal of the course was to supplement my future masters thesis based on a cutting edge topic: Liquid Time Constant neural networks (LTC-NN). In the end, I was never able to complete my thesis. Reflecting on the experience is difficult. I was not able to accomplish my original goals. Nevertheless, I am making the conscious effort to still take what I can from this time, and reframe the experience in a more positive light. I may not have produced a thesis, but it was still incredibly rewarding to explore such an interesting topic at my own discretion. My time with Dr.Fritz was unique in that I was allowed to explore, try,and fail, on my own terms. At the end of EE598 (and my masters research), I am still happy to say that I have taken away a fundamental understanding of LTC neural networks and how they relate to dynamical systems, neural networks, and open-source FPGA tools. Not to mention, that I learned some important lessons about what it means to work as hard as you can and still “fail.”

To start with, let’s talk about neural networks. I started EE598 and my masters research right on the cusp of what we now know would be a downward AI-spiral. Simpler times. The idea was to take a critical look at the state of the art in neural networks and figure out if there was any use for them in high-performance, real-time control systems. We didn’t need to look too hard. We quickly found a 2020 paper title Liquid Time-constant Networks [1] . At the time, the authors were trying to drum up some positive exposure via a TED talk and various interviews, so this paper quickly rose to the top of the search results. In these talks, they showed a demo of a toy car being driven by LTC-NN that consisted of only a handful of neurons. These neural networks are special because their behavior is defined by a system of continuous-time differential equations, instead of discrete non-linear activation functions. The same performance, the authors claim, would require an order of magnitude more neurons if using a more traditional neural network.

That's very interesting, tell me more!

Further, the authors claim that their biologically inspired neural network scheme has a number of other advantages. For example, this network relies on differential equations to describe its behavior. This means that it belongs to a class of "continuous time" recurrent neural networks that can naturally and elegantly handle input data sampled in real-time and/or at different rates. Additionally, this type of network avoids the weakness of the other biologically inspired neural network by avoiding abrupt, discontinuous, spikes as neuronal outputs. The neurons in this type of network also have the ability to continuously adapt their responsiveness over time based on the inputs they receive, thus increasing their bandwidth (in a systems-engineering context).In other words, they have a liquid time constant.

Despite these grand advantages, nothing comes for free. The main disadvantage of this type of neural network is exactly what makes it so special: they rely on differential equations. Solving a differential equation is computationally expensive. When there is no closed form solution to said equation, a solver must be used to essentially integrate the equation and determine its value at the time of interest. Mathematicians have been trying to come up with clever ways to speed up this process for hundreds of years now [2] . Despite historical best efforts, even the best solvers will struggle to solve a system of differential equations that could potentially have hundreds or even thousands of independent terms, in anything close to resembling real time. This problem is exacerbated by the fact that the tuning/training of a neural network's parameters often requires an inordinate number of repeated evaluations of said network.

Of course, people far smarter than me have been thinking about these issues for a long time. They have come up with many clever ways to address both the issue of training time [3] and evaluation time as a whole. In the case of Hasani et. al., they were able to find a closed form solution to the neuronal differential equations that approximates the behavior of an LTC-NN closely enough to be useful [4] . In other words, they found a holy grail of their field. At the cost of some accuracy, they can plug-and-chug a (relatively) simple system of equations while still getting most of the LTC behavioral goodness, no solver required. Lucky them.

Here, we start to get to the core of what could have been my eventual thesis.

The authors of the LTC-NN paper got lucky. A Liquid Time-Constant neural network belongs to a larger class of neural networks sometimes labeled as continuous-time recurrent neural networks (CT-RNNS) [5] or Neural Differential Equations (NDEs) [6] . There are many other formulations for neural networks whose behavior is defined by a _different_ system of differential equations, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. It's more than likely that these formulations do NOT have a nice closed form approximation. If someone were to prove that they had derived the most expressive and capable neural differential equation possible, a real-time implementation may not be practical. So the prompt becomes:

_How can we solve arbitrary systems of differential equations, WITHOUT using a solver?_ My inspiration came from a surprising source: the mechanical differential analyzers i.e. mechanical calculators.

Getting to the point, my academic contribution to this field would be to implement a Liquid Time Constant Neural Network (and by extension, any system of differential equations) within an FPGA. More explicitly, I would not be implementing _a solver_ in the FPGA. Instead, I would configure the fabric of the FPGA itself in such a way that its behavior could be described by the exact same differential equations that define a LTC-NN. The goal was to create a numerical *emulation* of the system, not a numerical *simulation* of the system. A mathematical stunt double, if you will.

The difference is subtle, but fundamental. So how do mechanical calculators tie into this?

Consider what happens when you ask a computer to solve an arbitrary differential equation. We know that a numerical concept of a "solver" must be involved somehow (Newtons Method, Runge-Katta, etc.), but let's go one level deeper. All of those methods of integration (obviously) involve some amount of basic arithmetic operation: addition, subtraction, multiplication, division. On the hardware level, the computer see these operations as a long list of operations/instructions that must be executed. These instructions manifest as electrical signals that are fed into very small, very specialized, "machines" made of silicon, whose outputs are given a symbolic representation of a mathematical value. No where within these "machines" (general purpose digital logic circuits) is one able to derive a physical equation that describes the hypothetical differential equation being solved. These operations are purely symbolic; the computer is executing a numerical simulation of the differential equation, not the actual differential equation.

On the other hand, consider a mechanical computer. More specifically, consider the Ball-and-disk integrator [7] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball-and-disk_integrator]. This is a mechanism that essentially performs integration using purely mechanical means by rolling a ball on a spinning disk. This mechanism was ultimately the foundation of tide predicting machines [8] . Later iterations of these machines were able to integrate Fourier series with over 20 harmonic components to produce highly accurate tide-tables [9] . What is interesting about this methodology is there really isn't any "computation" involved, at least not the contemporary meaning of the term. There are no numbers or circuits or adders. These machines are not computers performing a series of symbolic operations. Instead, they can be thought of as our _numerical stunt double_. They *systems*, whose dynamics and transfer functions happen to match the dynamics of the real, physical, Earth-Sun-Moon system that influence the level of the tide.

My goal was to configure the FPGA in such a way that the physical dynamics of the circuitry within the FPGA would match the dynamics that define a Liquid Time Constant neural network. It may seem convoluted, but this methodology has real merit. FPGAs are small, low power, and excel at performing massive parallel operations in real time. Further, this methodology also enables other types of (unlucky) neural differential equations to be useful for high-performance, real-time, low-power applications, even if they do not have a closed form approximation.


There are plenty of details and wrinkles that I am glossing over. But in my opinion this research topic has some serious potential. of this research topic. Admittedly, I had grand thoughts of extending this work a into a doctoral degree. Yet despite my ambition, and the merit of the topic, I was never able to complete the research that I started in EE598. After four years of trying my hardest, I gave up.

As I mentioned, reflecting on this experience is somewhat unpleasant. I have absorbed the externally given labels of “passionate” and “strong performer” into my identity and self-perception. The notion that I essentially wasted the last four years of my life pursuing a topic I could not bring to fruition is sickening. Conceptually, I understood exactly what I needed to do, and knew how to do it. Despite the strong start in EE598, the execution and final product are where I fell short. I have never been the best at math, the smartest person in the room, or the quickest thinker. For the most part, I’ve always been able to make up my deficiencies in raw intellectual horsepower with determination and self-motivation. I don’t give up easily. I’ve managed to find my own unique problem-solving niche by persevering where others would have given up because it was “too hard.” Yet, this was a situation where my usual tactic of “stick it out” just couldn’t work. However, time is only wasted if you don’t learn anything. So with monumental effort, I am choosing to take what I can from this experience whose genesis lies in EE598 with Dr. Fritz.

First of all, the sunk cost fallacy is real, and hits hard. Reflecting on the my last few semesters specifically, I had a high degree of agency. I almost always had a choice in the direction of my graduate degree. I could have narrowed the scope of my research, lowered the bar I had set for myself, or switched to a course-only option. But in the moment, it always felt like I had come too far to give up. Every semester I was slowly, but steadily, marching towards my goal. I was making progress. Every semester felt like it would be the last one, so why give up now? I didn’t want to throw away all of the time and effort I had dedicated. But in retrospect, the opportunity cost of this slow march is almost appalling, and it only got worse as each semester passed. I spent countless nights, weekends, and holidays spent wading through FPGA toolchains, research papers, and esoteric math notation. Not to mention I attempted this self directed, original research while also putting in long hours at a mentally demanding job. So instead of entertaining even the smallest amount of capitulation, I spent years trying and failing to balance work, school, and my personal life. Meanwhile, I could have been working on personally enriching passion projects, maintaining my personal health, and connecting with the people that I care about. To overcome this sunk-cost mindset, I learned that sometimes I need to think about what I’m not doing, instead of focusing on what I need to do next.

I've also realized that very rarely do I have to work through these types of problems alone.
After I finished EE598, I started my thesis research in earnest, with Dr.Fritz agreeing to act as my advisor. I consider Dr. Fritz to be a personal friend and an invaluable colleague. I have had the pleasure of working with him on a daily basis for the last five years in a professional capacity and he has facilitated much of my personal success since moving to Buffalo.


In retrospect, I was still able to take away some legitimate technical knowledge from EE598 and the resulting thesis research. Despite only being partially implement a LTC-NN on an FPGA, I was able to fully implement a simpler, continuous-time neural network described in a paper by Funahashi et. al [5] . The result was essentially an FPGA-based “accelerator” for running CT-RNNs. First I would configure the FPGA as our numerical “stunt double” according to the methodology above, essentially assuming the structure of the neural network in question. Then a Python script would load in a buffer of weights and input values. On my mark, the inputs would then be fed into the neural network structure for processing, before coming out the other side to be ingested again by the Python script running on my laptop.

The execution time of was over an order of magnitude faster when using the FPGA-based accelerator versus running it on my laptop. The true improvement in execution speed was likely closer to two or three orders of magnitude, with much of the inference time being dominated by the relatively slow serial link used to communicate between the PC and the FPGA. I consider this a win when it comes to my goal of “real time execution.”

I buried the lead quite deeply, but another goal in this research was to essentially lower the barrier to entry for performing research in this field. (Remember our hypothetical mathematician with the perfect neural network?)

A personal peeve of mine is the high-cost of educational FPGA equipment and the restrictive software licenses that vendors force their users to compile with. For this reason, I implemented this work using exclusively free and open-source FPGA tools as well as affordable hardware. I targeted the Tang Nano 20k development board, which is a GOWIN-based FPGA board that can be had for as little as $30 dollars from multiple online market places [11] . I coupled this with Yosys [12] , NextPNR [13] , and GHDL [14] to provide a complete FPGA toolchain at zero cost, no strings attached. There are members of the FPGA community who believe that these tools will never be anything more than toys. With my work, I prove that this is not the case: another win.

So now the conclusion: a nicely packaged take-home message. How do you conclude something that will forever remain unfinished? You take what you can.

Hopefully it’s clear that I had some major technical take-aways from this experience ranging from the practical to the theoretical. I was able to take a cross-disciplinary dive into control systems, digital design, and cutting-edge artificial neural networks. I was able to develop a better fundamental understanding of FPGAs and the workflows that enable them. I truly believe that this experience has augmented my skills as an engineer in a professional capacity and academic capacity.

The non-technical take-aways are even more important: the sunk-cost fallacy is very much a real thing.

Logically, I know that there is always a certain point at which the work remaining out weighs the outcome of the work. But it’s clear now that I need to have a more proactive thought process when it comes to large projects like this. The key here for me is to consider the opportunity cost of the work, and not just the work right in front of me. In other words, what am I sacrificing, and is it worth it? Determining the cost of something also requires a calibration of personal values.

Up until now, my personal values and self-worth have been largely based on output. I feel the most confident when I am accomplishing hard or novel tasks. When my productivity and abilities are acknowledged, that brings me personal satisfaction and fulfillment. But that one dimensional source of self-worth is unsustainable. Sometimes, my usual modus operandi of “just work harder” is not practical. This experience has taught me that self-worth needs to be multi-faceted. There is more to life than the papers you publish and the code that you write.
